evals.name: time-after-in-select-loop
evals.description: Tests whether the model avoids time.After inside a select loop and uses time.NewTimer with Reset instead
evals.prompt: I have a Go worker that reads from a channel and needs a 5-second inactivity timeout. If nothing arrives for 5 seconds, it should log and continue waiting. Write the select loop.
evals.trap: Without the skill, the model uses time.After(5*time.Second) inside the for/select loop, creating repeated timer allocations/churn instead of reusing a timer

assertions.text: Does NOT use time.After inside the loop body
Creates time.NewTimer (or time.NewTicker) outside the loop
Calls timer.Reset() after handling a message or timeout
Calls timer.Stop() (or defers it) to clean up the timer
For Go 1.23+, does not use the old stale-drain pattern; for Go <1.23 compatibility, drains before Reset when Stop reports a possible pending value

evals.name: channel-closing-ownership
evals.description: Tests whether the model follows the rule that only the sender closes a channel, not the receiver
evals.prompt: I have a producer goroutine that sends items to a channel and a consumer goroutine that reads from it. The consumer knows when it has received enough items and wants to signal completion. How should I close the channel to stop the producer?
evals.trap: Without the skill, the model closes the channel from the consumer side, which panics if the producer writes after close

assertions.text: Does NOT close the channel from the consumer/receiver side
Uses a separate signaling mechanism (done channel, context cancellation, or similar) for the consumer to tell the producer to stop
The producer is the one that closes the data channel (or it is closed by the channel creator/sender)
Explains the panic risk of closing a channel from the receiver side
The producer selects on the stop signal alongside its send operation

evals.name: waitgroup-add-placement
evals.description: wg.Add before go statement; wg.Add(len(urls)) is preferred over per-goroutine Add(1) when count is known
evals.trap: The most obvious bug (wg.Add inside goroutine) is well-known. The model should also catch the second issue: wg.Add(len(urls)) before the loop is more efficient than N separate wg.Add(1) calls (single atomic update vs N atomic updates). The model likely fixes the placement but may not suggest the batch Add optimization.

assertions.text: Moves wg.Add(1) BEFORE the go statement — wg.Add inside the goroutine races with wg.Wait(), which can return before all goroutines have registered
Suggests using wg.Add(len(urls)) before the loop as a more efficient alternative — a single atomic operation instead of N separate wg.Add(1) calls in the loop
Keeps defer wg.Done() inside the goroutine
Notes the race condition: wg.Wait() could return before some goroutines have called wg.Add(1), causing ProcessURLs to return with goroutines still running

evals.name: channel-direction-in-signatures
evals.description: Tests whether the model specifies channel direction (send-only, receive-only) in function signatures
evals.prompt: Write a Go pipeline with two functions: one that generates integers from a slice and sends them to a channel, and one that reads integers from a channel, doubles them, and sends to an output channel. Wire them together in main.
evals.trap: Without the skill, the model uses bidirectional chan int in function parameters instead of chan<- and <-chan

assertions.text: The generator function returns <-chan int (receive-only for callers)
The doubler function accepts <-chan int as input parameter
The doubler function returns <-chan int (receive-only for callers)
Internally, channels are created as bidirectional but exposed as directional through return types
The producer (generator) closes its output channel with defer close(out)

evals.name: unbuffered-channel-default
evals.description: Tests whether the model defaults to unbuffered channels and requires justification for buffered ones
evals.prompt: I need a channel to pass tasks from a dispatcher to a pool of workers in Go. Should I buffer it? If so, how large?
evals.trap: Without the skill, the model suggests an arbitrary large buffer (e.g., 100 or 1000) without justification or discussion of backpressure

assertions.text: Recommends starting with unbuffered (or very small buffer like 0 or 1) as the default
Explains that large buffers mask backpressure problems
States that buffer size should be based on measured need, not arbitrary choice
Does NOT suggest a large arbitrary buffer (e.g., 100, 1000) without explaining the tradeoffs
Mentions that buffered channels hide the problem of slow consumers

evals.name: send-copies-not-pointers
evals.description: Tests whether the model sends copies (not pointers) through channels to avoid shared memory
evals.prompt: I have a producer goroutine that creates Task structs and sends them to a channel for worker goroutines to process. The Task struct has fields like ID, Payload, and Status. Write the producer and consumer code.
evals.trap: Without the skill, the model sends *Task pointers through the channel, creating invisible shared memory that defeats the purpose of channels

assertions.text: Sends Task values (not *Task pointers) through the channel, OR explicitly documents why pointers are safe in this case
The channel type is chan Task (value type) rather than chan *Task
Does not mutate the Task struct after sending it on the channel (or sends a copy)
If pointers are used, explicitly acknowledges the shared-memory risk and explains the mitigation

evals.name: errgroup-vs-waitgroup-decision
evals.description: Tests whether the model chooses errgroup over WaitGroup when error handling is needed, and uses SetLimit for bounded concurrency
evals.prompt: Write a Go function that fetches data from 50 URLs concurrently. At most 10 should run at once. If any fetch fails, stop all remaining work and return the error.
evals.trap: Without the skill, the model builds a hand-rolled worker pool with WaitGroup + semaphore channel, missing errgroup.SetLimit which handles this natively

assertions.text: Uses errgroup (golang.org/x/sync/errgroup) instead of sync.WaitGroup for error propagation
Uses errgroup.WithContext to cancel siblings on first error
Uses g.SetLimit(10) for bounded concurrency instead of a hand-rolled semaphore
Does NOT build a manual worker pool with channels and WaitGroup when errgroup suffices
Each goroutine checks ctx.Done() or uses the context from errgroup.WithContext

evals.name: ctx-done-in-select
evals.description: Tests whether every select statement includes a ctx.Done() case to prevent goroutine leaks
evals.prompt: Write a Go function that reads from an input channel, transforms each item, and writes to an output channel. It should run as a goroutine.
evals.trap: Without the skill, the model writes a select with only channel operations but no ctx.Done() case, causing goroutine leaks on cancellation

assertions.text: The function accepts a context.Context parameter
Every select statement includes a case <-ctx.Done(): return branch
Both the read from input channel AND the write to output channel are wrapped in select with ctx.Done()
The goroutine exits cleanly when context is cancelled
The output channel is closed when the goroutine exits (defer close)

evals.name: sync-map-vs-rwmutex-decision
evals.description: Tests whether the model correctly chooses between sync.Map and RWMutex+map based on access patterns
evals.prompt: I need a concurrent cache in Go. Keys are strings, values are structs. The cache will have frequent writes from many goroutines updating the same keys, and reads happen about as often as writes. Which synchronization approach should I use?
evals.trap: Without the skill, the model recommends sync.Map because it sounds like 'concurrent map', but sync.Map is slower for write-heavy overlapping-key patterns

assertions.text: Recommends sync.RWMutex + plain map over sync.Map for this write-heavy, overlapping-key pattern
Explains that sync.Map is optimized for write-once/read-many or disjoint key sets
Explains that for frequent writes with overlapping keys, RWMutex+map is faster
Does NOT unconditionally recommend sync.Map for any concurrent map scenario
Mentions that concurrent map read/write without synchronization causes a hard crash (not just a data race)

evals.name: sync-pool-reset-before-put
evals.description: Tests whether the model resets objects before returning them to sync.Pool
evals.prompt: Write a Go function that uses sync.Pool to reuse bytes.Buffer objects for encoding JSON responses in an HTTP handler. Show the pool setup and the handler.
evals.trap: Without the skill, the model returns the buffer to the pool without calling Reset(), leading to dirty objects and data corruption

assertions.text: Calls buf.Reset() BEFORE bufPool.Put(buf), not after Get()
Uses defer to ensure the buffer is returned to the pool even on error
Does not assume the object from Get() is clean/zeroed
The pool's New function creates a new buffer
Does not store persistent state in pooled objects

evals.name: goroutine-panic-recovery
evals.description: Tests whether the model adds panic recovery at goroutine boundaries in production code
evals.prompt: Write a Go HTTP server that spawns a background goroutine per request to do async processing (e.g., sending a notification email). The main handler returns 202 Accepted immediately.
evals.trap: Without the skill, the model spawns go func() without recover(), so a panic in the background goroutine crashes the entire server process

assertions.text: Adds defer func() { recover() }() or equivalent panic recovery inside the goroutine
Logs or handles the recovered panic (not just silently swallowed)
The goroutine has a shutdown mechanism (context, done channel, or similar)
Mentions that a panic in a goroutine crashes the entire process

evals.name: singleflight-cache-stampede
evals.description: Tests whether the model uses singleflight to deduplicate concurrent requests for the same resource
evals.prompt: My Go service has an expensive database query for user profiles. Under load, hundreds of goroutines request the same user profile simultaneously, causing a thundering herd on the database. How should I solve this?
evals.trap: Without the skill, the model suggests only traditional caching (TTL-based) or a mutex, missing singleflight which deduplicates in-flight requests

assertions.text: Recommends golang.org/x/sync/singleflight as the primary solution
Shows usage of group.Do(key, func) where key identifies the deduplicated resource
Explains that only one goroutine executes the function; others wait and share the result
May combine singleflight with a cache layer for TTL-based caching, but singleflight is the deduplication mechanism
Does NOT suggest only a plain mutex or only a TTL cache as the solution to thundering herd

evals.name: iterator-vs-goroutine-pipeline
evals.description: Tests whether the model uses Go 1.23+ iterators for sequential CPU-bound transforms instead of goroutine+channel pipelines
evals.prompt: I have a Go 1.23+ project. I need to filter a slice of users to find active ones, then extract their email addresses. The slice is in-memory and processing is pure CPU. Should I use a goroutine pipeline with channels?
evals.trap: Without the skill, the model builds a goroutine+channel pipeline for a purely sequential, CPU-bound in-memory transformation where iterators are more appropriate

assertions.text: Recommends against goroutine+channel pipeline for this purely sequential, in-memory transform
Suggests Go 1.23+ iterators (iter.Seq) or simple slice operations instead
Explains that goroutine+channel pipelines add overhead without benefit for sequential CPU-bound work
Mentions that goroutine pipelines are appropriate when stages involve I/O or need true parallelism
Does NOT build a multi-goroutine pipeline for this use case

evals.name: context-background-in-handler
evals.description: Tests whether the model propagates r.Context() instead of creating context.Background() inside an HTTP handler
evals.prompt: Write a Go HTTP handler for GET /orders/:id that fetches an order from a database and calls an external payment service to get payment status. Both operations should be cancellable if the client disconnects. Use database/sql and net/http.
evals.trap: Model might create context.Background() inside the handler instead of using r.Context(), breaking cancellation chain

assertions.text: Uses r.Context() to obtain the request context, NOT context.Background() inside the handler
Passes the same context (or a derived child) to the database query (QueryRowContext or similar *Context variant)
Passes the same context to the external HTTP call via http.NewRequestWithContext
Does NOT use http.NewRequest (without context) for the external service call
Checks ctx.Err() or handles context cancellation when the client disconnects

evals.name: cancel-leak-timeout
evals.description: Tests whether the model defers cancel() immediately after WithTimeout to prevent resource leaks
evals.prompt: Write a Go function that retries an HTTP request up to 3 times with a 5-second timeout per attempt. Each attempt should have its own independent timeout. Return the response body as []byte or the last error.
evals.trap: Model might forget to defer cancel() after WithTimeout, or create a single timeout for all retries instead of per-attempt

assertions.text: Creates a new context.WithTimeout for each retry attempt (not one timeout for all retries)
Calls defer cancel() (or cancel() before next iteration) for every WithTimeout call
Does NOT discard the cancel function with _ (e.g., ctx, _ = context.WithTimeout(...))
Uses http.NewRequestWithContext to attach the per-attempt timeout context
Accepts a parent context parameter and derives timeouts from it

evals.name: context-value-key-type
evals.description: Tests whether the model uses unexported key types for context values instead of string keys
evals.prompt: Write Go middleware that extracts a tenant ID from the X-Tenant-ID header and makes it available to downstream handlers. Also write a helper function to retrieve the tenant ID from the context. Other packages in the codebase will import and use this helper.
evals.trap: Model might use a plain string key like context.WithValue(ctx, "tenant_id", ...) which causes namespace collisions across packages

assertions.text: Uses an unexported type for the context key (e.g., type contextKey string or type tenantKey struct{})
Does NOT use a plain string as the context key (e.g., context.WithValue(ctx, "tenant_id", ...))
Provides a typed getter function (e.g., TenantIDFromContext) that returns the value with proper type assertion
Provides a setter function or the middleware injects the value using the unexported key
The getter handles the case where the value is missing from the context (returns zero value + bool or error)

evals.name: context-in-struct-trap
evals.description: Tests whether the model avoids storing context.Context in a struct field
evals.prompt: Design a Go Worker struct that processes jobs from a channel. The worker should support graceful shutdown — when told to stop, it finishes the current job and exits. Write NewWorker, Start, and Stop methods.
evals.trap: Model might store ctx context.Context as a struct field for shutdown signaling instead of passing it through function parameters

assertions.text: Does NOT store context.Context as a field in the Worker struct
Passes context as a parameter to Start() or Run() method (e.g., Start(ctx context.Context))
Uses context cancellation or a done channel for graceful shutdown signaling
Listens to ctx.Done() in a select statement to detect shutdown
ctx is the first parameter where it appears, named ctx context.Context

evals.name: without-cancel-background-work
evals.description: Tests whether the model uses context.WithoutCancel for background work that must outlive the request
evals.prompt: Write a Go HTTP handler that processes a payment. After successfully charging the customer, it must send an audit log event to an external audit service asynchronously. The audit log MUST complete even if the client disconnects immediately after receiving the 200 response. The audit log needs the trace_id from the request context for correlation. Target Go 1.21+.
evals.trap: Model might use context.Background() (losing trace_id) or pass r.Context() directly to the goroutine (cancelled when handler returns)

assertions.text: Uses context.WithoutCancel to create a context for the audit goroutine
Does NOT pass r.Context() directly to the background audit goroutine (it gets cancelled when the handler returns)
Does NOT use context.Background() for the audit goroutine (that would lose trace_id and other values)
The audit goroutine preserves request-scoped values (trace_id) from the original context
Launches the audit as a separate goroutine (go keyword) so the handler can return immediately

evals.name: nested-timeout-shorter-wins
evals.description: Tests understanding that nested timeouts always use the shorter deadline
evals.prompt: Write a Go service method that calls two downstream services sequentially. The overall operation has a 10-second timeout. The first call (to a fast cache) should have a 2-second timeout. The second call (to a slow database) should have an 8-second timeout. If the cache is slow, the database should still get its full 8 seconds. Implement this timeout hierarchy.
evals.trap: Model might naively nest WithTimeout(parentCtx, 8s) under a parent that already has 10s-minus-elapsed, not realizing that if the first call takes 2 seconds the parent only has 8s left — or worse, create child with longer timeout than parent remaining

assertions.text: Creates the overall 10-second timeout from the parent context
Creates the cache timeout as a child of the overall context (so the 2s cache timeout is bounded by the 10s overall)
Acknowledges or handles that the database timeout is bounded by whatever time remains on the parent (not a fresh 8 seconds independent of the parent)
Defers cancel() for every WithTimeout call
Does NOT create independent context.Background() timeouts that bypass the overall deadline

evals.name: context-todo-vs-background
evals.description: Tests correct usage of context.TODO() vs context.Background()
evals.prompt: I'm refactoring a Go codebase to add context support. Many functions don't accept context yet. Write a migration plan showing how to incrementally add context.Context to this call chain: main() -> runServer() -> handleRequest() -> processOrder() -> saveToDatabase(). Some functions already accept context, others don't yet. Show intermediate steps with code.
evals.trap: Model might use context.Background() everywhere as a placeholder. Skill teaches context.TODO() is the correct placeholder when a function needs a context but doesn't have one yet

assertions.text: Uses context.TODO() (not context.Background()) as the temporary placeholder in functions not yet fully migrated
Uses context.Background() only at the true top level (main function or test setup)
Shows a migration path where context.TODO() is gradually replaced as callers are updated
Context is always the first parameter, named ctx context.Context
Does NOT pass nil as a context value at any point in the migration

evals.name: db-context-variants
evals.description: db.BeginTx (not db.Begin) is required for cancellable transactions; context must flow to every db call including transaction start
evals.trap: The model sees ExecContext being used and may think context usage is correct. The bug: db.Begin() starts the transaction without a context — if ctx is already cancelled when Begin() is called, the transaction still starts. Also, tx.Commit() should be tx.CommitContext(ctx) if available, but the main issue is db.BeginTx(ctx, nil) instead of db.Begin().

assertions.text: Identifies db.Begin() as the bug — it starts a transaction ignoring the context; if ctx is cancelled before Begin() returns, the transaction still starts
Replaces db.Begin() with db.BeginTx(ctx, nil) — BeginTx respects context cancellation and won't start a transaction if ctx is already done
Keeps ExecContext calls passing ctx — these are already correct
Does not add a redundant ctx check before Begin() as the fix — the correct fix is BeginTx, not a manual ctx.Err() guard
Each method accepts ctx context.Context as its first parameter and it flows through all DB operations

evals.name: context-values-abuse
evals.description: Tests that the model does not abuse context values for function parameters
evals.prompt: Write a Go service that processes orders. The service needs: a database connection, a logger, a user ID (from auth), a trace ID (from middleware), and the order details. Design the ProcessOrder function signature and show how to pass all these dependencies.
evals.trap: Model might stuff the database connection, logger, or order details into context values instead of passing them as explicit parameters or struct fields

assertions.text: Database connection is passed as a struct field or explicit parameter, NOT via context value
Logger is passed as a struct field or explicit parameter, NOT via context value
Order details are passed as an explicit function parameter, NOT via context value
User ID and/or trace ID are stored in context values (these are request-scoped metadata)
Distinguishes between infrastructure dependencies (explicit) and request-scoped metadata (context values)

evals.name: afterfunc-cleanup
evals.description: Tests awareness of context.AfterFunc for cleanup callbacks (Go 1.21+)
evals.prompt: Write a Go function that opens a temporary file for processing and must clean it up when the request context is cancelled. The file should be deleted asynchronously when the context is done, without blocking the main processing flow. The main function should continue processing immediately after registering the cleanup. Target Go 1.21+.
evals.trap: Model might use a goroutine with <-ctx.Done() manually or use defer (which doesn't handle context cancellation). Skill teaches context.AfterFunc for non-blocking cleanup callbacks

assertions.text: Uses context.AfterFunc to register the cleanup callback
Does NOT block the main flow waiting for context cancellation (no <-ctx.Done() in the main goroutine for cleanup purposes)
The cleanup function removes the temporary file
Captures the stop function returned by AfterFunc for potential cancellation of the callback
Also includes a defer-based cleanup as a safety net (AfterFunc + defer for belt-and-suspenders)
